title: Narada's glimpse: bhakti, supreme love
hookLine: a servant's boy hears the sages' stories, glimpses the Lord once, and spends his life singing; the sutras credited to him call it supreme love
carry: bhakti: supreme love that wants nothing else

cards: Long before he was the wandering sage with the vina, Narada says, he was a servant's little boy. One rainy season, a group of wandering sages stayed where his mother worked.

The boy served them, ate what they left with their blessing, and listened while they told stories of Krishna, every day, for months. Something in him turned toward what he heard. Then the sages moved on.

teach.b: Narada tells this himself, to Vyasa, in the first book of the Bhagavata Purana. Not long after, his mother died, bitten by a snake, and the boy, with no one left, walked north.
In a forest, under a tree, he turned his mind toward the Lord the way the sages had taught him, and for a moment the Lord appeared in his heart.
Then it was gone. He tried and tried to see it again. A voice told him gently: you won't see me again in this life; I showed myself so your longing would grow.
He spent the rest of that life singing the Lord's names, and was born again as Narada, who wanders the worlds with his vina.
So the short book of sayings credited to Narada comes from someone who learned love the long way.
The Narada Bhakti Sutras open like a manual: atha, now, then, we will explain bhakti.
The second sutra gives the whole definition: toward this one, it is of the form of supreme love, parama prema. Commentators take this one to be the Lord. Then the sutras say what such love does.
Having it, a person becomes complete and satisfied; they want nothing else, grieve for nothing, hate nothing. That's the teaching of bhakti: love for God so full that other wanting goes quiet.
The word comes from bhaj, to share in, and to serve. And notice where Narada's love began: not in a temple, but in hearing stories near people who loved.
That's still how many Hindus grow it, in satsang, good company, and kirtan, singing the names together.

how: Some Hindus, especially in Vaishnava communities, study the Narada Bhakti Sutras in satsang groups, reading a few sutras and a commentary together. Bhakti itself is lived in puja, kirtan, japa and service offered to a chosen form of God.

o: loving devotion, which the sutras call supreme love
a strict rulebook for performing temple rituals
a calm that comes from giving up all feeling

games.q: narada and the sutras — tap the pairs.
p: then a voice: let longing grow
the root: to share, to serve

s: Narada was always a great sage with a vina
in the Bhagavata he tells Vyasa he was once a servant's boy who heard the sages' stories.
the second sutra defines bhakti as supreme love
parama prema, toward this one; commentators take it as the Lord.
the sutras say bhakti makes you want more and more
having it, a person wants nothing else, grieves for nothing, hates nothing.

games.q: you're the servant's boy. you've seen the Lord once, and now you can't. a voice says you won't again in this life. what do you do?
o: give up: it was only a dream.
spend your life singing the names, longing.
try harder until you force it back.
games.why: the voice says the glimpse was given so longing would grow. he sings the names for the rest of that life, and is born as Narada.

practice: If you pray, sing or hum one name of God you love, the way Narada did, a few times, slowly; if your family has a bhajan, use its first line. If you don't, bring to mind someone or something you love deeply.
Then notice what the sutra describes: does the wanting quiet down a little? You don't need to make anything happen. Rest near what you love, and watch.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Devotion, from bhaj, to share and to serve. The Narada Bhakti Sutras call it supreme love.

orig.note: Sanskrit bhakti, devotion, from the root bhaj, to share, partake, serve; a devotee is a bhakta.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti, supreme love that wants nothing else. Tomorrow, the gopis, who miss Krishna so much they teach a wise man. That's day six hundred ninety-three.
